entries.7bee662d8366b99b95f82dceca28514d625416e7: <div sID="gen9250" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Job.3" sID="Job.3"/> <div eID="gen9250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9251" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9252" type="x-p"/> "You have heard of the patience of Job," says the apostle, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.11">Jam. v. 11</reference>. So we have, and of his impatience too. We wondered that a man should be so patient as he was (<reference osisRef="Job.1.1-Job.2.13">ch. i. and ii.</reference>), but we wonder also that a good man should be so impatient as he is in this chapter, where we find him cursing his day, and, in passion, I. Complaining that he was born, <reference osisRef="Job.3.1-Job.3.10">ver. 1-10</reference>. II. Complaining that he did not die as soon as he was born, <reference osisRef="Job.3.11-Job.3.19">ver. 11-19</reference>. III. Complaining that his life was now continued when he was in misery, <reference osisRef="Job.3.20-Job.3.26">ver. 20-26</reference>. In this it must be owned that Job sinned with his lips, and it is written, not for our imitation, but our admonition, that he who thinks he stands may take heed lest he fall.
entries.7f6fe17db4c84d4cffc0906c601d6c0cc4267f3e: <div eID="gen9252" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9251" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Job Curses His Day. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9253" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> After this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Job spake, and said, <hi type="super">3</hi> Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night <hi type="italic">in which</hi> it was said, There is a man child conceived. <hi type="super">4</hi> Let that day be darkness; let not God regard it from above, neither let the light shine upon it. <hi type="super">5</hi> Let darkness and the shadow of death stain it; let a cloud dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it. <hi type="super">6</hi> As <hi type="italic">for</hi> that night, let darkness seize upon it; let it not be joined unto the days of the year, let it not come into the number of the months. <hi type="super">7</hi> Lo, let that night be solitary, let no joyful voice come therein. <hi type="super">8</hi> Let them curse it that curse the day, who are ready to raise up their mourning. 9 Let the stars of the twilight thereof be dark; let it look for light, but <hi type="italic">have</hi> none; neither let it see the dawning of the day: <hi type="super">10</hi> Because it shut not up the doors of my <hi type="italic">mother's</hi> womb, nor hid sorrow from mine eyes. <div eID="gen9253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9254" type="x-p"/> Long was Job's heart hot within him; and, while he was musing, the fire burned, and the more for being stifled and suppressed. At length he spoke with his tongue, but not such a good word as David spoke after a long pause: <hi type="italic">Lord, make me to know my end,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.39.3-Ps.39.4">Ps. xxxix. 3, 4</reference>. Seven days the prophet Ezekiel sat down astonished with the captives, and then (probably on the sabbath day) <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord came to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.15-Ezek.3.16">Ezek. iii. 15, 16</reference>. So long Job and his friends sat thinking, but said nothing; <hi type="italic">they</hi> were afraid of speaking what they thought, lest they should grieve him, and <hi type="italic">he</hi> durst not give vent to his thoughts, lest he should offend them. They came to comfort him, but, finding his afflictions very extraordinary, they began to think comfort did not belong to him, suspecting him to be a hypocrite, and therefore they said nothing. But losers think they may have leave to speak, and therefore Job first gives vent to his thoughts. Unless they had been better, it would however have been well if he had kept them to himself. In short, he cursed his day, the day of his birth, wished he had never been born, could not think or speak of his own birth without regret and vexation. Whereas men usually observe the annual return of their birth-day with rejoicing, he looked upon it as the unhappiest day of the year, because the unhappiest of his life, being the inlet into all his woe. Now, <div eID="gen9254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9255" type="x-p"/> I. This was bad enough. The extremity of his trouble and the discomposure of his spirits may excuse it in part, but he can by no means be justified in it. Now he has forgotten the good he was born to, the lean kine have eaten up the fat ones, and he is filled with thoughts of the evil only, and wishes he had never been born. The prophet Jeremiah himself expressed his painful sense of his calamities in language not much unlike this: <hi type="italic">Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me!</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.15.10">Jer. xv. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Cursed be the day wherein I was born,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.20.14">Jer. xx. 14</reference>, &c. We may suppose that Job in his prosperity had many a time blessed God for the day of his birth, and reckoned it a happy day; yet now he brands it with all possible marks of infamy. When we consider the iniquity in which we were conceived and born we have reason enough to reflect with sorrow and shame upon the day of our birth, and to say that the <hi type="italic">day of our death,</hi> by which we are <hi type="italic">freed from sin</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.7">Rom. vi. 7</reference>), is far <hi type="italic">better.</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Eccl. vii. 1</reference>. But to curse the day of our birth because then we entered upon the calamitous scene of life is to quarrel with the God of nature, to despise the dignity of our being, and to indulge a passion which our own calm and sober thoughts will make us ashamed of. Certainly there is no condition of life a man can be in in this world but he may in it (if it be not his own fault) so honour God, and work out his own salvation, and make sure a happiness for himself in a better world, that he will have no reason at all to wish he had never been born, but a great deal of reason to say that he had his being to good purpose. Yet it must be owned, if there were not another life after this, and divine consolations to support us in the prospect of it, so many are the sorrows and troubles of this that we might sometimes be tempted to say that we were <hi type="italic">made in vain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.47">Ps. lxxxix. 47</reference>), and to wish we had never been. There are those in hell who with good reason wish they had never been born, as Judas, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.24">Matt. xxvi. 24</reference>. But, on this side hell, there can be no reason for so vain and ungrateful a wish. It was Job's folly and weakness to curse his day. We must say of it, This was his infirmity; but good men have sometimes failed in the exercise of those graces which they have been most eminent for, that we may understand that when they are said to be <hi type="italic">perfect</hi> it is meant that they were upright, not that they were sinless. <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Let us observe it, to the honour of the spiritual life above the natural, that though many have cursed the day of their first birth, never any cursed the day of their new-birth, nor wished they never had had grace, and the Spirit of grace, given them. Those are the most excellent gifts, above life and being itself, and which will never be a burden. <div eID="gen9255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9256" type="x-p"/> II. Yet it was not so bad as Satan promised himself. Job cursed his day, but he did not curse his God—was weary of his life, and would gladly have parted with that, but not weary of his religion; he resolutely cleaves to that, and will never let it go. The dispute between God and Satan concerning Job was not whether Job had his infirmities, and whether he was subject to like passions as we are (that was granted), but whether he was a hypocrite, who secretly hated God, and if he were provoked, would show his hatred; and, upon trial, it proved that he was no such man. Nay, all this may consist with his being a pattern of patience; for, though he did thus speak unadvisedly with his lips, yet both before and after he expressed great submission and resignation to the holy will of God and repented of his impatience; he condemned himself for it, and therefore God did not condemn him, nor must we, but watch the more carefully over ourselves, lest we sin after the similitude of this transgression. <div eID="gen9256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9257" type="x-p"/> 1. The particular expressions which Job used in cursing his day are full of poetical fancy, flame, and rapture, and create as much difficulty to the critics as the thing itself does to the divines: we need not be particular in our observations upon them. When he would express his passionate wish that he had never been, he falls foul upon the day, and wishes, <div eID="gen9257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9258" type="x-p"/> (1.) That earth might forget it: <hi type="italic">Let it perish</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.3.3">v. 3</reference>); <hi type="italic">let it not be joined to the days of the year,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.3.6">v. 6</reference>. "Let it be not only not inserted in the calendar in red letters, as the day of the king's nativity useth to be" (and Job was a king, <reference osisRef="Job.29.25">ch. xxix. 25</reference>), "but let it be erased and blotted out, and buried in oblivion. Let not the world know that ever such a man as I was born into it, and lived in it, who am made such a spectacle of misery." <div eID="gen9258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9259" type="x-p"/> (2.) That Heaven might frown upon it: <hi type="italic">Let not God regard it from above,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.3.4">v. 4</reference>. "Every thing is indeed as it is with God; that day is honourable on which he puts honour, and which he distinguishes and crowns with his favour and blessing, as he did the seventh day of the week; but let my birthday never be so honoured; let it be <hi type="italic">nigro carbone notandus—marked as with a black coal</hi> for an evil day by him that determines the times before appointed. The father and fountain of light appointed the greater light to rule the day and the less lights to rule the night; but let that want the benefit of both." [1.] <hi type="italic">Let that day be darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.3.4">v. 4</reference>); and, if the light of the day be darkness, <hi type="italic">how great is that darkness!</hi> how terrible! because then we look for light. Let the gloominess of the day represent Job's condition, whose sun went down at noon. [2.] As for that night too, let it want the benefit of moon and stars, and <hi type="italic">let darkness seize upon it,</hi> thick darkness, darkness that may be felt, which will not befriend the repose of the night by its silence, but rather disturb it with its terrors. <div eID="gen9259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9260" type="x-p"/> (3.) That all joy might forsake it: "Let it be a melancholy night, solitary, and not a merry night of music and dancing. <hi type="italic">Let no joyful voice come therein</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.3.7">v. 7</reference>); let it be a long night, and not <hi type="italic">see the eye-lids of the morning</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.3.9">v. 9</reference>), which bring joy with them." <div eID="gen9260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9261" type="x-p"/> (4.) That all curses might follow it (<reference osisRef="Job.3.8">v. 8</reference>): "Let none ever desire to see it, or bid it welcome when it comes, but, on the contrary, <hi type="italic">let those curse it that curse the day.</hi> Whatever day any are tempted to curse, let them at the same time bestow one curse upon my birth-day, particularly those that make it their trade to raise up mourning at funerals with their ditties of lamentation. Let those that curse the day of the death of others in the same breath curse the day of my birth." Or those who are so fierce and daring as to be ready to raise up the <hi type="italic">Leviathan</hi> (for that is the word here), who, being about to strike the whale or crocodile, curse it with the bitterest curse they can invent, hoping by their incantations to weaken it, and so to make themselves master of it. Probably some such custom might there be used, to which our divine poet alludes. "Let it be as odious as <hi type="italic">the day wherein men bewail the greatest misfortune,</hi> or the time <hi type="italic">wherein they see the most dreadful apparition;</hi>" so bishop Patrick, I suppose taking the Leviathan here to signify the devil, as others do, who understand it of the curses used by conjurors and magicians in raising the devil, or when they have raised a devil that they cannot lay. <div eID="gen9261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9262" type="x-p"/> 2. But what is the ground of Job's quarrel with the day and night of his birth? It is <hi type="italic">because it shut not up the doors of his mother's womb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.3.10">v. 10</reference>. See the folly and madness of a passionate discontent, and how absurdly and extravagantly it talks when the reins are laid on the neck of it. Is this Job, who was so much admired for his wisdom that <hi type="italic">unto him men gave ear, and kept silence at his counsel,</hi> and <hi type="italic">after his words they spoke not again?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.29.21-Job.29.22">ch. xxix. 21, 11</reference>. Surely his wisdom failed him, (1.) When he took so much pains to express his desire that he had never been born, which, at the best was a vain wish, for it is impossible to make that which has been not to have been. (2.) When he was so liberal of his curses upon a day and a night that could not be hurt, or made any the worse for his curses. (3.) When he wished a thing so very barbarous to his own mother as that she had not brought him forth when her full time had come, which must inevitably have been her death, and a miserable death. (4.) When he despised the goodness of God to him in giving him a being (such a being, so noble and excellent a life, such a life, so far above that of any other creature in this lower world), and undervalued the gift, as not worth the acceptance, only because <hi type="italic">transit cum onere—it was clogged with a proviso of trouble,</hi> which now at length came upon him, after many years' enjoyment of its pleasures. What a foolish thing it was to wish that his eyes had never seen the light, that so they might not have seen sorrow, which yet he might hope to see through, and beyond which he might see joy! Did Job believe and hope that he should <hi type="italic">in his flesh see God at the latter day</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.19.26">ch. xix. 26</reference>), and yet would he wish he had never had a being capable of such a bliss, only because, for the present, he had sorrow in the flesh? God by his grace arm us against this foolish and hurtful lust of impatience.
entries.741ef54d9c2222cdf8bed6dc825affed8ddc4c90: <div eID="gen9262" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Complaint of Life. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9263" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Why died I not from the womb? <hi type="italic">why</hi> did I <hi type="italic">not</hi> give up the ghost when I came out of the belly? <hi type="super">12</hi> Why did the knees prevent me? or why the breasts that I should suck? <hi type="super">13</hi> For now should I have lain still and been quiet, I should have slept: then had I been at rest, <hi type="super">14</hi> With kings and counsellors of the earth, which built desolate places for themselves; <hi type="super">15</hi> Or with princes that had gold, who filled their houses with silver: <hi type="super">16</hi> Or as a hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants <hi type="italic">which</hi> never saw light. <hi type="super">17</hi> There the wicked cease <hi type="italic">from</hi> troubling; and there the weary be at rest. <hi type="super">18</hi> <hi type="italic">There</hi> the prisoners rest together; they hear not the voice of the oppressor. <hi type="super">19</hi> The small and great are there; and the servant <hi type="italic">is</hi> free from his master. <div eID="gen9263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9264" type="x-p"/> Job, perhaps reflecting upon himself for his folly in wishing he had never been born, follows it, and thinks to mend it, with another, little better, that he had died as soon as he was born, which he enlarges upon in these verses. When our Saviour would set forth a very calamitous state of things he seems to allow such a saying as this, <hi type="italic">Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that never bore, and the paps which never gave suck</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.29">Luke xxiii. 29</reference>); but blessing the barren womb is one thing and cursing the fruitful womb is another! It is good to make the best of afflictions, but it is not good to make the worst of mercies. Our rule is, <hi type="italic">Bless, and curse not.</hi> Life is often put for all good, and death for all evil; yet Job here very absurdly complains of life and its supports as a curse and plague to him, and covets death and the grave as the greatest and most desirable bliss. Surely Satan was deceived in Job when he applied that maxim to him, <hi type="italic">All that a man hath will he give for his life;</hi> for never any man valued life at a lower rate than he did. <div eID="gen9264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9265" type="x-p"/> I. He ungratefully quarrels with life, and is angry that it was not taken from him as soon as it was given him (<reference osisRef="Job.3.11-Job.3.12">v. 11, 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Why died not I from the womb?</hi> See here, 1. What a weak and helpless creature man is when he comes into the world, and how slender the thread of life is when it is first drawn. We are ready to die from the womb, and to breathe our last as soon as we begin to breathe at all. We can do nothing for ourselves, as other creatures can, but should drop into the grave if the knees did not prevent us; and the lamp of life, when first lighted, would go out of itself if the breasts given us, that we should suck, did not supply it with fresh oil. 2. What a merciful and tender care divine Providence took of us at our entrance into the world. It was owing to this that we <hi type="italic">died not from the womb</hi> and did not <hi type="italic">give up the ghost when we came out of the belly.</hi> Why were we not cut off as soon as we were born? Not because we did not deserve it. Justly might such weeds have been plucked up as soon as they appeared; justly might such cockatrices have been crushed in the egg. Nor was it because we did, or could, take any care of ourselves and our own safety: no creature comes into the world so shiftless as man. It was not our might, or the power of our hand, that preserved us these beings, but God's power and providence upheld our frail lives, and his pity and patience spared our forfeited lives. It was owing to this that the knees prevented us. Natural affection is put into parents' hearts by the hand of the God of nature: and hence it was that the blessings of the breast attended those of the womb. 3. What a great deal of vanity and vexation of spirit attends human life. If we had not a God to serve in this world, and better things to hope for in another world, considering the faculties we are endued with and the troubles we are surrounded with, we should be strongly tempted to wish that we had <hi type="italic">died from the womb,</hi> which would have prevented a great deal both of sin and misery. <div eID="gen9265" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen9266"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9267"/>He that is born to-day, and dies to-morrow,<l eID="gen9267" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9268"/>Loses some hours of joy, but months of sorrow.<l eID="gen9268" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen9266"/> <div sID="gen9269" type="x-p"/> 4. The evil of impatience, fretfulness, and discontent. When they thus prevail they are unreasonable and absurd, impious and ungrateful. To indulge them is a slighting and undervaluing of God's favour. How much soever life is embittered, we must say, "It was of the Lord's mercies that we died not from the womb, that we were not consumed." Hatred of life is a contradiction to the common sense and sentiments of mankind, and to our own at any other time. Let discontented people declaim ever so much against life, they will be loth to part with it when it comes to the point. When the old man in the fable, being tired with his burden, threw it down with discontent and called for Death, and Death came to him and asked him what he would have with him, he then answered, "Nothing, but to help me up with my burden." <div eID="gen9269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9270" type="x-p"/> II. He passionately applauds death and the grave, and seems quite in love with them. To desire to die that we may be with Christ, that we may be free from sin, and that we may be <hi type="italic">clothed upon with our house which is from heaven,</hi> is the effect and evidence of grace; but to desire to die only that we may be quiet in the grave, and delivered from the troubles of this life, savours of corruption. Job's considerations here may be of good use to reconcile us to death when it comes, and to make us easy under the arrest of it; but they ought not to be made use of as a pretence to quarrel with life while it is continued, or to make us uneasy under the burdens of it. It is our wisdom and duty to make the best of that which is, be it living or dying, and so to <hi type="italic">live to the Lord</hi> and <hi type="italic">die to the Lord,</hi> and to be his in both, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.8">Rom. xiv. 8</reference>. Job here frets himself with thinking that if he had but died as soon as he was born, and been carried from the womb to the grave, 1. His condition would have been as good as that of the best: I would have been (says he, <reference osisRef="Job.3.14">v. 14</reference>) <hi type="italic">with kings and counsellors of the earth,</hi> whose pomp, power, and policy, cannot set them out of the reach of death, nor secure them from the grave, nor distinguish theirs from common dust in the grave. Even princes, who had gold in abundance, could not with it bribe Death to overlook them when he came with commission; and, though they filled their houses with silver, yet they were forced to leave it all behind them, no more to return to it. Some, by the <hi type="italic">desolate places</hi> which the kings and counsellors are here said <hi type="italic">to build for themselves,</hi> understand the sepulchres or monuments they prepared for themselves in their life-time; as Shebna (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.16">Isa. xxii. 16</reference>) <hi type="italic">hewed himself out a sepulchre;</hi> and by the gold which the princes had, and the silver with which they filled their houses, they understand the treasures which, they say, it was usual to deposit in the graves of great men. Such arts have been used to preserve their dignity, if possible, on the other side death, and to keep themselves from lying even with those of inferior rank; but it will not do: death is, and will be, an irresistible leveller. <hi type="italic">Mors sceptra ligonibus æquat—Death mingles sceptres with spades. Rich and poor meet together</hi> in the grave; and there a <hi type="italic">hidden untimely birth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.3.16">v. 16</reference>), a child that either never saw light or but just opened its eyes and peeped into the world, and, not liking it, closed them again and hastened out of it, lies as soft and easy, lies as high and safe, as kings and counsellors, and princes, that had gold. "And therefore," says Job, "would I had lain there in the dust, rather than to lie here in the ashes!" 2. His condition would have been much better than now it was (<reference osisRef="Job.3.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Then should I have lain still, and been quiet,</hi> which now I cannot do, I cannot be, but am still tossing and unquiet; then <hi type="italic">I should have slept,</hi> whereas now sleep departeth from my eyes; <hi type="italic">then had I been at rest,</hi> whereas now I am restless." Now that life and immortality are brought to a much clearer light by the gospel than before they were placed in good Christians can give a better account than this of the gain of death: "Then should I have been present with the Lord; then should I have seen his glory face to face, and no longer through a glass darkly." But all that poor Job dreamed of was rest and quietness in the grave out of the fear of evil tidings and out of the feeling of sore boils. <hi type="italic">Then should I have been quiet;</hi> and had he kept his temper, his even easy temper still, which he was in as recorded in the two foregoing chapters, entirely resigned to the holy will of God and acquiescing in it, he might have been quiet now; his soul, at least, might have dwelt at ease, even when his body lay in pain, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.13">Ps. xxv. 13</reference>. Observe how finely he describes the repose of the grave, which (provided the soul also be at rest in God) may much assist our triumphs over it. (1.) Those that now are troubled will there be out of the reach of trouble (<reference osisRef="Job.3.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">There the wicked cease from troubling.</hi> When persecutors die they can no longer persecute; their <hi type="italic">hatred and envy</hi> will then <hi type="italic">perish.</hi> Herod had vexed the church, but, when he became a prey for worms, he ceased from troubling. When the persecuted die they are out of the danger of being any further troubled. Had Job been at rest in his grave, he would have had no disturbance from the Sabeans and Chaldeans, none of all his enemies would have created him any trouble. (2.) Those that are now toiled will there see the period of their toils. <hi type="italic">There the weary are at rest.</hi> Heaven is more than a rest to the souls of the saints, but the grave is a rest to their bodies. Their pilgrimage is a weary pilgrimage; sin and the world they are weary of; their services, sufferings, and expectations, they are wearied with; but in the grave they <hi type="italic">rest from all their labours,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.13">Rev. xiv. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.23">Isa. lvii. 23</reference>. They are easy there, and make no complaints; there believers sleep in Jesus. (3.) Those that were here enslaved are there at liberty. Death is the prisoner's discharge, the relief of the oppressed, and the servant's manumission (<reference osisRef="Job.3.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">There the prisoners,</hi> though they walk not at large, yet they <hi type="italic">rest together,</hi> and are not put to work, to grind in that prison-house. They are no more insulted and trampled upon, menaced and terrified, by their cruel task-masters: <hi type="italic">They hear not the voice of the oppressor.</hi> Those that were here doomed to perpetual servitude, that could call nothing their own, no, not their own bodies, are there no longer under command or control: <hi type="italic">There the servant is free from his master,</hi> which is a good reason why those that have power should use it moderately, and those that are in subjection should bear it patiently, yet a little while. (4.) Those that were at a vast distance from others are there upon a level (<reference osisRef="Job.3.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">The small and great are there,</hi> there the same, there all one, all alike free among the dead. The tedious pomp and state which attend the great are at an end there. All the inconveniences of a poor and low condition are likewise over; death and the grave know no difference. <div eID="gen9270" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen9271"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9272"/>Levelled by death, the conqueror and the slave,<l eID="gen9272" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9273"/>The wise and foolish, cowards and the brave,<l eID="gen9273" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9274"/>Lie mixed and undistinguished in the grave. Sir <hi type="small-caps">R. Blackmore</hi> .
entries.6d9cbfe196a641d6e8273226b64e718c84c19e7a: <l eID="gen9274" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen9271"/> <div sID="gen9275" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter <hi type="italic">in</hi> soul; <hi type="super">21</hi> Which long for death, but it <hi type="italic">cometh</hi> not; and dig for it more than for hid treasures; <hi type="super">22</hi> Which rejoice exceedingly, <hi type="italic">and</hi> are glad, when they can find the grave? <hi type="super">23</hi> <hi type="italic">Why is light given</hi> to a man whose way is hid, and whom God hath hedged in? 24 For my sighing cometh before I eat, and my roarings are poured out like the waters. <hi type="super">25</hi> For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me. <hi type="super">26</hi> I was not in safety, neither had I rest, neither was I quiet; yet trouble came. <div eID="gen9275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9276" type="x-p"/> Job, finding it to no purpose to wish either that he had not been born or had died as soon as he was born, here complains that his life was now continued and not cut off. When men are set on quarrelling there is no end of it; the corrupt heart will carry on the humour. Having cursed the day of his birth, here he courts the day of his death. The beginning of this strife and impatience is as the letting forth of water. <div eID="gen9276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9277" type="x-p"/> I. He thinks it hard, in general, that miserable lives should be prolonged (<reference osisRef="Job.3.20-Job.3.22">v. 20-22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherefore is light in life given to those that are bitter in soul?</hi> Bitterness of soul, through spiritual grievances, makes life itself bitter. <hi type="italic">Why doth he give light?</hi> (so it is in the original): he means <hi type="italic">God,</hi> yet does not name him, though the devil had said, "He will curse thee to thy face;" but he tacitly reflects on the divine Providence as unjust and unkind in continuing life when the comforts of life are removed. Life is called <hi type="italic">light,</hi> because pleasant and serviceable for walking and working. It is candle-light; the longer it burns the shorter it is, and the nearer to the socket. This light is said to be given us; for, if it were not daily renewed to us by a fresh gift, it would be lost. But Job reckons that to those who are in misery it is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">doron adoron</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">gift and no gift,</hi> a gift that they had better be without, while the light only serves them to see their own misery by. Such is the vanity of human life that it sometimes becomes a vexation of spirit; and so alterable is the property of death that, though dreadful to nature, it may become desirable even to nature itself. He here speaks of those, 1. Who long for death, when they have out-lived their comforts and usefulness, are burdened with age and infirmities, with pain or sickness, poverty or disgrace, and yet it comes not; while, at the same time, it comes to many who dread it and would put it far from them. The continuance and period of life must be according to God's will, not according to ours. It is not fit that we should be consulted how long we would live and when we would die; our times are in a better hand than our own. 2. Who <hi type="italic">dig for it as for hidden treasures,</hi> that is, would give any thing for a fair dismission out of this world, which supposes that <hi type="italic">then</hi> the thought of men's being their own executioners was not so much as entertained or suggested, else those who longed for it needed not take much pains for it, they might soon come at it (as Seneca tells them) if they are pleased. 3. Who bid it welcome, and <hi type="italic">are glad</hi> when they can find the grave and see themselves stepping into it. If the miseries of this life can prevail, contrary to nature, to make death itself desirable, shall not much more the hopes and prospects of a better life, to which death is our passage, make it so, and set us quite above the fear of it? It may be a sin to long for death, but I am sure it is no sin to long for heaven. <div eID="gen9277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9278" type="x-p"/> II. He thinks himself, in particular, hardly dealt with, that he might not be eased of his pain and misery by death when he could not get ease in any other way. To be thus impatient of life for the sake of the troubles we meet with is not only unnatural in itself, but ungrateful to the giver of life, and argues a sinful indulgence of our own passion and a sinful inconsideration of our future state. Let it be our great and constant care to get ready for another world, and then let us leave it to God to order the circumstances of our removal thither as he thinks fit: "Lord, when and how thou pleasest;" and this with such an indifference that, if he should refer it to us, we would refer it to him again. Grace teaches us, in the midst of life's greatest comforts, to be willing to die, and, in the midst of its greatest crosses, to be willing to live. Job, to excuse himself in this earnest desire which he had to die, pleads the little comfort and satisfaction he had in life. <div eID="gen9278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9279" type="x-p"/> 1. In his present afflicted state troubles were continually felt, and were likely to be so. He thought he had cause enough to be weary of living, for, (1.) He had no comfort of his life: <hi type="italic">My sighing comes before I eat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.3.24">v. 24</reference>. The sorrows of life prevented and anticipated the supports of life; nay, they took away his appetite for his necessary food. His griefs returned as duly as his meals, and affliction was his daily bread. Nay, so great was the extremity of his pain and anguish that he did not only sigh, but roar, and his <hi type="italic">roarings were poured out like the waters</hi> in a full and constant stream. Our Master was acquainted with grief, and we must expect to be so too. (2.) He had no prospect of bettering his condition: <hi type="italic">His way was hidden,</hi> and God had <hi type="italic">hedged him in,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.3.23">v. 23</reference>. He saw no way open of deliverance, nor knew he what course to take; his way was <hi type="italic">hedged up with thorns,</hi> that he could not find his path. See <reference osisRef="Job.23.8">ch. xxiii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.7">Lam. iii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen9279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9280" type="x-p"/> 2. Even in his former prosperous state troubles were continually feared; so that <hi type="italic">then</hi> he was never easy, <reference osisRef="Job.3.25-Job.3.26">v. 25, 26</reference>. He knew so much of the vanity of the world, and the troubles to which, of course, he was born, that he was <hi type="italic">not in safety, neither had he rest</hi> then. That which made his grief now the more grievous was that he was not conscious to himself of any great degree either of negligence or security in the day of his prosperity, which might provoke God thus to chastise him. (1.) He had not been negligent and unmindful of his affairs, but kept up such a fear of trouble as was necessary to the maintaining of his guard. He was afraid for his children when they were feasting, lest they should offend God (<reference osisRef="Job.1.5">ch. i. 5</reference>), afraid for his servants lest they should offend his neighbours; he took all the care he could of his own health, and managed himself and his affairs with all possible precaution; yet all would not do. (2.) He had not been secure, nor indulged himself in ease and softness, had not trusted in his wealth, nor flattered himself with the hopes of the perpetuity of his mirth; yet trouble came, to convince and remind him of the vanity of the world, which yet he had not forgotten when he lived at ease. Thus his way was hidden, for he knew not wherefore God contended with him. Now this consideration, instead of aggravating his grief, might rather serve to alleviate it. Nothing will make trouble easy so much as the testimony of our consciences for us, that, in some measure, we did our duty in a day of prosperity; and an expectation of trouble will make it sit the lighter when it comes. The less it is a surprise the less it is a terror.  <chapter eID="Job.3"/> <div eID="gen9280" type="x-p"/>

entries.f1a6bea635549fb0aa7deb82d42f3f4985835f46: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4491"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen6506" type="x-p"/> THE POEM OR DEBATE ITSELF (Job 3:2-42:6). FIRST SERIES IN IT (Job 3:<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.22">1-14:22</reference>). JOB FIRST (<reference osisRef="Job.3.1-Job.3.26">Job 3:1-26</reference>).<div eID="gen6506" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.3.1-Job.3.19">Job 3:1-19</reference>. Job Curses the Day of His Birth and Wishes for Death.</title> <div sID="gen6507" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4491"/><hi type="bold">1. opened his mouth--</hi>The Orientals speak seldom, and then sententiously; hence this formula expressing deliberation and gravity (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.2">Psa 78:2</reference>). He formally began.<div eID="gen6507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cursed his day--</hi>the strict Hebrew word for "cursing:" not the same as in <reference osisRef="Job.1.5">Job 1:5</reference>. Job cursed his birthday, but not his God. <div eID="gen6508" type="x-p"/>
entries.a83dff5d28b5bd9fc23b876ce76efff4cbd7b6ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4492"/><div sID="gen6509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4492"/><hi type="bold">2. spake--</hi>Hebrew, "answered," that is, not to any actual question that preceded, but to the question virtually involved in the case. His outburst is singularly wild and bold (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.14">Jr 20:14</reference>). To desire to die so as to be free from sin is a mark of grace; to desire to die so as to escape troubles is a mark of corruption. He was ill-fitted to die who was so unwilling to live. But his trials were greater, and his light less, than ours. <div eID="gen6509" type="x-p"/>
entries.4307eacc487fd57bc7f9c3e0cdbc9f5d35094fae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4493"/><div sID="gen6510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4493"/><hi type="bold">3. the night in which--</hi>rather "the night which said." The words in italics are not in the Hebrew. Night is personified and poetically made to speak. So in <reference osisRef="Job.3.7">Job 3:7</reference>, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.19.2">Psa 19:2</reference>. The birth of a male in the East is a matter of joy; often not so of a female. <div eID="gen6510" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e6a750fcc566270be198fcce67638d153f737f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4494"/><div sID="gen6511" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4494"/><hi type="bold">4. let not God regard it--</hi>rather, more poetically, "seek it out." "Let not God stoop from His bright throne to raise it up from its dark hiding-place." The curse on the day in <reference osisRef="Job.3.3">Job 3:3</reference>, is amplified in <reference osisRef="Job.3.4">Job 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.3.5">5</reference>; that on the night, in <reference osisRef="Job.3.6-Job.3.10">Job 3:6-10</reference>. <div eID="gen6511" type="x-p"/>
entries.eeba418e8ce113257b4be92e0fc43fb602d8c71e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4495"/><div sID="gen6512" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4495"/><hi type="bold">5. Let ... the shadow of death--</hi>("deepest darkness," <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Is 9:2</reference>).<div eID="gen6512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stain it--</hi>This is a later sense of the verb [Gesenius]; better the old and more poetic idea, "Let darkness (the ancient night of chaotic gloom) resume its rights over light (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Ge 1:2</reference>), and claim that day as its own."<div eID="gen6513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a cloud--</hi>collectively, a gathered mass of dark clouds.<div eID="gen6514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the blackness of the day terrify it--</hi>literally, "the obscurations"; whatever darkens the day [Gesenius]. The verb in Hebrew expresses sudden terrifying. May it be suddenly affrighted at its own darkness. Umbreit explains it as "magical incantations that darken the day," forming the climax to the previous clauses; <reference osisRef="Job.3.8">Job 3:8</reference> speaks of "cursers of the day" similarly. But the former view is simpler. Others refer it to the poisonous simoom wind. <div eID="gen6515" type="x-p"/>
entries.64d734c8e68852699863a0bd7d68408bec341e45: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4496"/><div sID="gen6516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4496"/><hi type="bold">6. seize upon it--</hi>as its prey, that is, utterly dissolve it.<div eID="gen6516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6517" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">joined unto the days of the year--</hi>rather, by poetic personification, "Let it not rejoice in the circle of days and nights and months, which form the circle of years." <div eID="gen6517" type="x-p"/>
entries.fecb44bf1d248c454afffb84c2625d531d70eb78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4497"/><div sID="gen6518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4497"/><hi type="bold">7. solitary--</hi>rather, "unfruitful." "Would that it had not given birth to me." <div eID="gen6518" type="x-p"/>
entries.d50068ef9dae8b1d6e81ba8c0eb957e4d333a80e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4498"/><div sID="gen6519" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4498"/><hi type="bold">8. them ... curse the day--</hi>If "mourning" be the right rendering in the latter clause of this verse, these words refer to the hired mourners of the dead (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.17">Jr 9:17</reference>). But the Hebrew for "mourning" elsewhere always denotes an animal, whether it be the crocodile or some huge serpent (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Is 27:1</reference>), such as is meant by "leviathan." Therefore, the expression, "cursers of day," refers to magicians, who were believed to be able by charms to make a day one of evil omen. (So Balaam, <reference osisRef="Num.22.5">Nu 22:5</reference>). This accords with Umbreit's view (<reference osisRef="Job.3.7">Job 3:7</reference>); or to the Ethiopians and Atlantes, who "used to curse the sun at his rising for burning up them and their country" [Herodotus]. Necromancers claimed power to control or rouse wild beasts at will, as do the Indian serpent-charmers of our day (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.5">Psa 58:5</reference>). Job does not say they had the power they claimed; but, supposing they had, may they curse the day. Schuttens renders it by supplying words as follows:--Let those that are ready for anything, call it (the day) the raiser up of leviathan, that is, of a host of evils. <div eID="gen6519" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ddd0d4d1d143b1ab92192ec81bf2e02b2295b98: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4499"/><div sID="gen6520" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4499"/><hi type="bold">9. dawning of the day--</hi>literally, "eyelashes of morning." The Arab poets call the sun the eye of day. His early rays, therefore, breaking forth before sunrise, are the opening eyelids or eyelashes of morning. <div eID="gen6520" type="x-p"/>
entries.01cb2bb8233ca676a3454ecb330077ea8b55a3f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4500"/><div sID="gen6521" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4500"/><hi type="bold">12. Why did the knees prevent me?--</hi>Old English for "anticipate my wants." The reference is to the solemn recognition of a new-born child by the father, who used to place it on his knees as his own, whom he was bound to rear (<reference osisRef="Gen.30.3">Ge 30:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.50.23">50:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.12">Is 66:12</reference>). <div eID="gen6521" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca57e5644f2bc291ee05569550587ecfa244c755: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4501"/><div sID="gen6522" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4501"/><hi type="bold">13. lain ... quiet ... slept--</hi>a gradation. I should not only have lain, but been quiet, and not only been quiet, but slept. Death in Scripture is called "sleep" (<reference osisRef="Ps.13.3">Psa 13:3</reference>); especially in the New Testament, where the resurrection-awakening is more clearly set forth (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.51">1Co 15:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.14">1Th 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.10">5:10</reference>). <div eID="gen6522" type="x-p"/>
entries.557a03de1e90bcf6220e8eabe949fb19932a8ccd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4502"/><div sID="gen6523" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4502"/><hi type="bold">14. With kings ... which built desolate places for themselves--</hi>who built up for themselves what proved to be (not palaces, but) ruins! The wounded spirit of Job, once a great emir himself, sick of the vain struggles of mortal great men, after grandeur, contemplates the palaces of kings, now desolate heaps of ruins. His regarding the repose of death the most desirable end of the great ones of earth, wearied with heaping up perishable treasures, marks the irony that breaks out from the black clouds of melancholy [Umbreit]. The "for themselves" marks their selfishness. Michaelis explains it weakly of mausoleums, such as are found still, of stupendous proportions, in the ruins of Petra of Idumea. <div eID="gen6523" type="x-p"/>
entries.7dfd9b9a7ed232cc8938b5c9e12d7af19fbe47f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4503"/><div sID="gen6524" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4503"/><hi type="bold">15. filled their houses with silver--</hi>Some take this to refer to the treasures which the ancients used to bury with their dead. But see <reference osisRef="Job.3.26">Job 3:26</reference>. <div eID="gen6524" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a274d63d8e1d225141fbd60d64e7066735a054b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4504"/><div sID="gen6525" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4504"/><hi type="bold">16. untimely birth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.58.8">Psa 58:8</reference>); preferable to the life of the restless miser (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.3-Eccl.6.5">Ec 6:3-5</reference>). <div eID="gen6525" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7b12ce002e0c6bdf738c098f2a156f5eac10298: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4505"/><div sID="gen6526" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4505"/><hi type="bold">17. the wicked--</hi>the original meaning, "those ever restless," "full of desires" (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.20">Is 57:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen6526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the weary--</hi>literally, "those whose strength is wearied out" (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.13">Re 14:13</reference>). <div eID="gen6527" type="x-p"/>
entries.925eb98c672e30a61dceb21c0f904f3a8b7f37a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4506"/><div sID="gen6528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4506"/><hi type="bold">18. There the prisoners rest--</hi>from their chains. <div eID="gen6528" type="x-p"/>
entries.72a12cbe6502b63a87576268236f41a87b4252ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4507"/><div sID="gen6529" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4507"/><hi type="bold">19. servant--</hi>The slave is there manumitted from slavery. <div eID="gen6529" type="x-p"/>
entries.c29e8cd9612ef1ece32ed35d4191df9f820bbf62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4508"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.3.20-Job.3.26">Job 3:20-26</reference>. He Complains of Life because of His Anguish.</title> <div sID="gen6530" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4508"/><hi type="bold">20. Wherefore giveth he light--</hi>namely, God; often omitted reverentially (<reference osisRef="Job.24.23">Job 24:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.9">Ec 9:9</reference>). Light, that is, life. The joyful light ill suits the mourners. The grave is most in unison with their feelings. <div eID="gen6530" type="x-p"/>
entries.209dfe0830fd60c989e52651431e55ff8f1421db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4509"/><div sID="gen6531" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4509"/><hi type="bold">23. whose way is hid--</hi>The picture of Job is drawn from a wanderer who has lost his way, and who is hedged in, so as to have no exit of escape (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.6">Ho 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.7">La 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.9">9</reference>). <div eID="gen6531" type="x-p"/>
entries.3de7690bc9267dcac3b989f320b117ab029de857: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4510"/><div sID="gen6532" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4510"/><hi type="bold">24. my sighing cometh before I eat--</hi>that is, prevents my eating [Umbreit]; or, conscious that the effort to eat brought on the disease, Job must sigh before eating [Rosenmuller]; or, sighing takes the place of good (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.3">Psa 42:3</reference>) [Good]. But the first explanation accords best with the text.<div eID="gen6532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my roarings are poured out like the waters--</hi>an image from the rushing sound of water streaming. <div eID="gen6533" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf304c7e273d99541bcfe584b6b4dd23b61482d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4511"/><div sID="gen6534" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4511"/><hi type="bold">25. the thing which I ... feared is come upon me--</hi>In the beginning of his trials, when he heard of the loss of one blessing, he feared the loss of another; and when he heard of the loss of that, he feared the loss of a third.<div eID="gen6534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which I was afraid of is come unto me--</hi>namely, the ill opinion of his friends, as though he were a hypocrite on account of his trials. <div eID="gen6535" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf459476f979e54669274c3365cad359290a8907: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4512"/><div sID="gen6536" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4512"/><hi type="bold">26. I was not in safety ... yet trouble came--</hi>referring, not to his former state, but to the beginning of his troubles. From that time I had no rest, there was no intermission of sorrows. "And" (not, "yet") a fresh trouble is coming, namely, my friends' suspicion of my being a hypocrite. This gives the starting-point to the whole ensuing controversy. <chapter eID="Job.3"/>

entries.4a82ff32f4c50fbf864680be6cfbc2b2f8bb5d44: <div eID="gen15921" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15922" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15923" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15923" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15922" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15924" type="x-p"/> Job curses the day of his birth, and regrets that he ever saw the light, <reference osisRef="Job.3.1-Job.3.12">Job 3:1-12</reference>. Describes the empire of death and its inhabitants, <reference osisRef="Job.3.13-Job.3.19">Job 3:13-19</reference>. Regrets that he is appointed to live in the midst of sorrows, for the calamities which he feared had overtaken him, vv.20-26. <div eID="gen15924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15925" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen15925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15926" type="x-p"/> After this opened Job his mouth - After the seven days' mourning was over, there being no prospect of relief, Job is represented as thus cursing the day of his birth. Here the poetic part of the book begins; for most certainly there is nothing in the preceding chapters either in the form or spirit of Hebrew poetry. It is easy indeed to break the sentences into hemistichs; but this does not constitute them poetry: for, although Hebrew poetry is in general in hemistichs, yet it does not follow that the division of narrative into hemistichs must necessarily constitute it poetry. <div eID="gen15926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15927" type="x-p"/> In many cases the Asiatic poets introduce their compositions with prose narrative; and having in this way prepared the reader for what he is to expect, begin their deevans, cassidehs, gazels, etc. This appears to be the plan followed by the author of this book. Those who still think, after examining the structure of those chapters, and comparing them with the undoubted poetic parts of the book, that they also, and the ten concluding verses, are poetry, have my consent, while I take the liberty to believe most decidedly the opposite. <div eID="gen15927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15928" type="x-p"/> Cursed his day - That is, the day of his birth; and thus he gave vent to the agonies of his soul, and the distractions of his mind. His execrations have something in them awfully solemn, tremendously deep, and strikingly sublime. But let us not excuse all the things which he said in his haste, and in the bitterness of his soul, because of his former well established character of patience. He bore all his privations with becoming resignation to the Divine will and providence: but now, feeling himself the subject of continual sufferings, being in heaviness through manifold temptation, and probably having the light of God withdrawn from his mind, as his consolations most undoubtedly were, he regrets that ever he was born; and in a very high strain of impassioned poetry curses his day. We find a similar execration to this in Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.20.14-Jer.20.18">Jer 20:14-18</reference>, and in other places; which, by the way, are no proofs that the one borrowed from the other; but that this was the common mode of Asiatic thinking, speaking, and feeling, on such occasions.
entries.f3c83f0fd59d4a36b37235999ede0c8f3dbf5b8c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen15928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15929" type="x-p"/> There is a man-child conceived - The word הרה harah signifies to conceive; yet here, it seems, it should be taken in the sense of being born, as it is perfectly unlikely that the night of conception should be either distinctly known or published.
entries.559bab14c766b036f6deddefa003b9e3b8eb326a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen15929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15930" type="x-p"/> Let that day be darkness - The meaning is exactly the same with our expression, "Let it be blotted out of the calendar." However distinguished it may have been, as the birthday of a man once celebrated for his possessions, liberality, and piety, let it no longer be thus noted; as he who was thus celebrated is now the sport of adversity, the most impoverished, most afflicted, and most wretched of human beings. <div eID="gen15930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15931" type="x-p"/> Let not God regard it from above - אל ידרשהו al yidreshehu, "Let Him not require it" - let Him not consider it essential to the completion of the days of the year; and therefore he adds, neither let the light shine upon it. If it must be a part of duration, let it not be distinguished by the light of the sun.
entries.2e748b22b8a3008183f0c824a275c5da8d7bf5f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen15931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15932" type="x-p"/> Let darkness and the shadow of death stain it - יגאלהו yigaluhu, "pollute or avenge it," from גאל gaal, to vindicate, avenge, etc.; hence גאל goel, the nearest of kin, whose right it was to redeem an inheritance, and avenge the death of his relative by slaying the murderer. Let this day be pursued, overtaken, and destroyed. Let natural darkness, the total privation of the solar light, rendered still more intense by death's shadow projected over it, seize on and destroy this day, εκλαβοι αυτην, Septuagint; alluding, perhaps, says Mr. Parkhurst, to the avenger of blood seizing the offender. <div eID="gen15932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15933" type="x-p"/> Let a cloud dwell upon it - Let the dymme cloude fall upon it - Coverdale. Let the thickest clouds have there their dwelling-place - let that be the period of time on which they shall constantly rest, and never be dispersed. This seems to be the import of the original, תשכן עליו אננה tishcan alaiv ananah. Let it be the place in which clouds shall be continually gathered together, so as to be the storehouse of the densest vapors, still in the act of being increasingly condensed. <div eID="gen15933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15934" type="x-p"/> Let the blackness of the day terrify it - And let it be lapped in with sorrowe. - Coverdale. This is very expressive: lap signifies to fold up, or envelope any particular thing with fold upon fold, so as to cover it everywhere and secure it in all points. Leaving out the semicolon, we had better translate the whole clause thus: "Let the thickest cloud have its dwelling-place upon it, and let the bitterness of a day fill it with terror." A day similar to that, says the Targum, in which Jeremiah was distressed for the destruction of the house of the sanctuary; or like that in which Jonah was cast into the sea of Tarsis; such a day as that on which some great or national misfortune has happened: probably in allusion to that in which the darkness that might be felt enveloped the whole land of Egypt, and the night in which the destroying angel slew all the first-born in the land.
entries.29a4bdd967712c0182920b8347f927d1540a270e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen15934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15935" type="x-p"/> As for that night, let darkness seize upon it - I think the Targum has hit the sense of this whole verse: "Let darkness seize upon that night; let it not be reckoned among the annual festivals; in the number of the months of the calendar let it not be computed." Some understand the word אפל ophel as signifying a dark storm; hence the Vulgate, tenebrosus turbo, "a dark whirlwind." And hence Coverdale, Let the darck storme overcome that night, let it not be reckoned amonge the dayes off the yeare, nor counted in the monethes. Every thing is here personified; day, night, darkness, shadow of death, cloud, etc.; and the same idea of the total extinction of that portion of time, or its being rendered ominous and portentous, is pursued through all these verses, from the third to the ninth, inclusive. The imagery is diversified, the expressions varied, but the idea is the same.
entries.591fd6331f3e8597349bc816e9a6c9ed3bf5b49e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen15935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15936" type="x-p"/> Lo, let that night be solitary - The word הנה hinneh, behold, or lo, is wanting in one of De Rossi's MSS., nor is it expressed in the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, or Arabic. The word גלמוד galmud, which we translate solitary, is properly Arabic. From ghalama or jalama, signifying to cut off, make bare, amputate, comes jalmud, a rock, a great stone; and jalameedet, weight, a burden, trouble, from which we may gather Job's meaning: "Let that night be grievous, oppressive, as destitute of good as a bare rock is of verdure." The Targum gives the sense, In that night let there be tribulation. <div eID="gen15936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15937" type="x-p"/> Let no joyful voice come therein - Let there be no choirs of singers; no pleasant music heard; no dancing or merriment. The word רננה renanah signifies any brisk movement, such as the vibration of the rays of light, or the brisk modulation of the voice in a cheerful ditty. The Targum has, Let not the crowing of the rural or wild cock resound in it. Let all work be intermitted; let there be no sportive exercises, and let all animals be totally silent.
entries.6b8c59e5148b46ab9019fa0ef7e624518f4c7d7f: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen15937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15938" type="x-p"/> Let them curse it that curse the day - This translation is scarcely intelligible. I have waded through a multitude of interpretations, without being able to collect from them such a notion of the verse as could appear to me probable. Schultens, Rosenmller, and after them Mr. Good, have labored much to make it plain. They think the custom of sorcerers who had execrations for peoples, places, things, days, etc., is here referred to; such as Balaam, Elymas, and many others were: but I cannot think that a man who knew the Divine Being and his sole government of the world so well as Job did, would make such an allusion, who must have known that such persons and their pretensions were impostors and execrable vanities. I shall give as near a translation as I can of the words, and subjoin a short paraphrase: יקבהו אררי יום העתידימערר לויתן yikkebuhu orerey yom haathidim orer livyathan; "Let them curse it who detest the day; them who are ready to raise up the leviathan." That is, Let them curse my birthday who hate daylight, such as adulterers, murderers, thieves, and banditti, for whose practices the night is more convenient; and let them curse it who, being like me weary of life, are desperate enough to provoke the leviathan, the crocodile, to tear them to pieces. This version is nearly the same as that given by Coverdale. Let them that curse the daye give it their curse also, then those that be ready to rayse up leviathan. By leviathan some understand the greatest and most imminent dangers; and others, the devil, whom the enchanters are desperate enough to attempt to raise by their incantations. Calmet understands the whole to be spoken of the Atlantes, a people of Ethiopia, who curse the sun because it parches their fields and their bodies; and who fearlessly attack, kill, and eat the crocodile. This seems a good sense.
entries.4744eb0b36da5f3ae01ca5fa21d0d4557cc5b9f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen15938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15939" type="x-p"/> Let the stars of the twilight thereof - The stars of the twilight may here refer to the planets Venus, Jupiter, Mars, and Mercury, as well as to the brighter fixed stars. <div eID="gen15939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15940" type="x-p"/> Let it look for light - Here the prosopopoeia or personification is still carried on. The darkness is represented as waiting for the lustre of the evening star, but is disappointed; and these for the aurora or dawn, but equally in vain. He had prayed that its light, the sun, should not shine upon it, <reference osisRef="Job.3.4">Job 3:4</reference>; and here he prays that its evening star may be totally obscured, and that it might never see the dawning of the day. Thus his execration comprehends every thing that might irradiate or enliven it.
entries.b88a66ff2e5827b9e0ec60de72e59c98b4d5388d: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen15940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15941" type="x-p"/> Because it shut not up the doors - Here is the reason why he curses the day and the night in which he was conceived and born; because, had he never been brought into existence, he would never have seen trouble. It seems, however, very harsh that he should have wished the destruction of his mother, in order that his birth might have been prevented; and I rather think Job's execration did not extend thus far. The Targum understands the passage as speaking of the umbilical cord, by which the fetus is nourished in its mother's womb: had this been shut up, there must have been a miscarriage, or he must have been dead born; and thus sorrow would have been hidden from his eyes. This seeming gloss is much nearer the letter and spirit of the Hebrew than is generally imagined. I shall quote the words: כי לא סגר דלתי בטני ki lo sagar dalthey bitni, because it did not shut up the doors of my belly. This is much more consistent with the feelings of humanity, than to wish his mother's womb to have been his grave.
entries.7a5ee084b1eb9a1c7026b0944ff4b73906a463eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen15941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15942" type="x-p"/> Why died I not from the womb - As the other circumstance did not take place, why was I not still-born, without the possibility of reviviscence? or, as this did not occur, why did I not die as soon as born? These three things appear to me to be clearly intended here: - <div eID="gen15942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15943" type="x-p"/> 1. Dying in the womb, or never coming to maturity, as in the case of an abortion. <div eID="gen15943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15944" type="x-p"/> 2. Being still-born, without ever being able to breathe. <div eID="gen15944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15945" type="x-p"/> 3. Or, if born alive, dying within a short time after. And to these states he seems to refer in the following verses.
entries.5f46df85b823dd6b55b2be420c71253e3b88ab24: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen15945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15946" type="x-p"/> Why did the knees prevent me? - Why was I dandled on the knees? Why was I nourished by the breasts? In either of the above cases I had neither been received into a mother's lap, nor hung upon a mother's breasts.
entries.5d5d43333b45bb77263980247b64e062243593ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen15946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15947" type="x-p"/> For now should I have lain still - In that case I had been insensible; quiet - without these overwhelming agitations; slept - unconscious of evil; been at rest - been out of the reach of calamity and sorrow.
entries.2e7d90bf0659a350d30589eb61bac5df4d355719: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen15947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15948" type="x-p"/> With kings and counsellors of the earth - I believe this translation to be perfectly correct. The counsellors, יעצי yoatsey, I suppose to mean the privy council, or advisers of kings; those without whose advice kings seldom undertake wars, expeditions, etc. These mighty agitators of the world are at rest in their graves, after the lives of commotion which they have led among men: most of whom indeed have been the troublers of the peace of the globe. <div eID="gen15948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15949" type="x-p"/> Which built desolate places - Who erect mausoleums, funeral monuments, sepulchral pyramids, etc., to keep their names from perishing, while their bodies are turned to corruption. I cannot think, with some learned men, that Job is here referring to those patriotic princes who employed themselves in repairing the ruins and desolations which others had occasioned. His simple idea is, that, had he died from the womb, he would have been equally at rest, neither troubling nor troubled, as those defunct kings and planners of wars and great designs are, who have nothing to keep even their names from perishing, but the monuments which they have raised to contain their corrupting flesh, moldering bones, and dust.
entries.63dbc16e51821e93ca441cd6b0dea4e22c6284ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen15949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15950" type="x-p"/> Or with princes that had gold - Chief or mighty men, lords of the soil, or fortunate adventurers in merchandise, who got gold in abundance, filled their houses with silver, left all behind, and had nothing reserved for themselves but the empty places which they had made for their last dwelling, and where their dust now sleeps, devoid of care, painful journeys, and anxious expectations. He alludes here to the case of the covetous, whom nothing can satisfy, as an Asiatic writer has observed, but the dust that fills his mouth when laid in the grave - Saady.
entries.10960c1bbe64c95d3822d13a82fa21d24b54c7be: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen15950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15951" type="x-p"/> Or as a hidden untimely birth - An early miscarriage, which was scarcely perceptible by the parent herself; and in this case he had not been - he had never had the distinguishable form of a human being, whether male or female. <div eID="gen15951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15952" type="x-p"/> As infants - Little ones; those farther advanced in maturity, but miscarried long before the time of birth.
entries.953d323076d99a9b540462617d6751d07478c98e: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen15952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15953" type="x-p"/> There the wicked cease - In the grave the oppressors of men cease from irritating, harassing, and distressing their fellow creatures and dependents. <div eID="gen15953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15954" type="x-p"/> And there the weary be at rest - Those who were worn out with the cruelties and tyrannies of the above. The troubles and the troubled, the restless and the submissive, the toils of the great and the labors of the slave, are here put in opposition.
entries.d963be5230f2b813ec6bbeba885abe3cecd0bc6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen15954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15955" type="x-p"/> The prisoners rest together - Those who were slaves, feeling all the troubles, and scarcely tasting any of the pleasures of life, are quiet in the grave together; and the voice of the oppressor, the hard, unrelenting task-master, which was more terrible than death, is heard no more. They are free from his exactions, and his mouth is silent in the dust. This may be a reference to the Egyptian bondage. The children of Israel cried by reason of their oppressors or task-masters.
entries.acdd01dd54b25b6f102edb36af41384178114032: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen15955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15956" type="x-p"/> The small and great are there - All sorts and conditions of men are equally blended in the grave, and ultimately reduced to one common dust; and between the bond and free there is no difference. The grave is "The appointed place of rendezvous, where all These travelers meet." <div eID="gen15956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15957" type="x-p"/> Equality is absolute among the sons of men in their entrance into and exit from the world: all the intermediate state is disparity. All men begin and end life alike; and there is no difference between the king and the cottager. <div eID="gen15957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15958" type="x-p"/> A contemplation of this should equally humble the great and the small. <div eID="gen15958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15959" type="x-p"/> The saying is trite, but it is true: - <div eID="gen15959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15960" type="x-p"/> Pallida mors aequo pulsat pede pauperum tabernas, <div eID="gen15960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15961" type="x-p"/> Regumque turres. <div eID="gen15961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15962" type="x-p"/> Hor. Odar. lib. i., Od. iv., ver. 13. "With equal pace impartial Fate <div eID="gen15962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15963" type="x-p"/> Knocks at the palace as the cottage gate." <div eID="gen15963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15964" type="x-p"/> Death is that state,"Where they an equal honor shareWho buried or unburied are.Where Agamemnon knows no moreThan Irus he contemn'd before.Where fair Achilles and Thersites lie,Equally naked, poor, and dry." <div eID="gen15964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15965" type="x-p"/> And why do not the living lay these things to heart? <div eID="gen15965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15966" type="x-p"/> There is a fine saying in Seneca ad Marciam, cap. 20, on this subject, which may serve as a comment on this place: Mors-servitutem invito domino remittit; haec captivorum catenas levat; haec e carcere eduxit, quos exire imperium impotens vetuerat. Haec est in quo nemo humilitatem suam sensit; haec quae nulli paruit; haec quae nihil quicquam alieno fecit arbitrio. Haec, ubi res communes fortuna male divisit, et aequo jure genitos alium alii donavit, exaequat omnia. - "Death, in spite of the master, manumits the slave. It loosens the chains of the prisoners. It brings out of the dungeon those whom impotent authority had forbidden to go at large. This is the state in which none is sensible of his humiliation. Death obeys no man. It does nothing according to the will of another. It reduces, by a just law, to a state of equality, all who in their families and circumstances had unequal lots in life."
entries.981f82270991ee4c1aa3f13df7e9361d4c4f5542: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen15966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15967" type="x-p"/> Wherefore is light given - Why is life granted to him who is incapable of enjoying it, or of performing its functions?
entries.7b5e89009d3434305995c5c21639892e5962f24f: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen15967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15968" type="x-p"/> Which long for death - They look to it as the end of all their miseries; and long more for a separation from life, than those who love gold do for a rich mine.
entries.6df8886c04e9fdab64440a1044cd6a82098780e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen15968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15969" type="x-p"/> Which rejoice exceedingly - Literally, They rejoice with joy, and exult when they find the grave. There is a various reading here in one of Kennicott's MSS., which gives a different sense. Instead of who rejoice, אלי גיל eley gil, with Joy, it has אלי גל eley gal, who rejoice at the Tomb, and exult when they find the grave.
entries.7549c4009d24b6878f6f4b7c68abef9af6d1385e: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen15969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15970" type="x-p"/> To a man whose way is hid - Who knows not what is before him in either world, but is full of fears and trembling concerning both. <div eID="gen15970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15971" type="x-p"/> God hath hedged in? - Leaving him no way to escape; and not permitting him to see one step before him. There is an exact parallel to this passage in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.7">Lam 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.9">Lam 3:9</reference> : He hath hedged me about that I cannot get out. He hath inclosed my ways with hewn stone. Mr. Good translates the verse thus: To the man whose path is broken up, and whose futurity God hath overwhelmed. But I cannot see any necessity for departing from the common text, which gives both an easy and a natural sense.
entries.610429def8d5e6e8599ac96cc22bc06c838dcae6: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen15971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15972" type="x-p"/> For my sighing cometh - Some think that this refers to the ulcerated state of Job's body, mouth, hands, etc. He longed for food, but was not able to lift it to his mouth with his hands, nor masticate it when brought thither. This is the sense in which Origen has taken the words. But perhaps it is most natural to suppose that he means his sighing took away all appetite, and served him in place of meat. There is the same thought in <reference osisRef="Psa.42.3">Psa 42:3</reference> : My tears have been my meat day and night; which place is not an imitation of Job, but more likely Job an imitation of it, or, rather, both an imitation of nature. <div eID="gen15972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15973" type="x-p"/> My roarings are poured out - My lamentations are like the noise of the murmuring stream, or the dashings of the overswollen torrent.
entries.5fe5c041a841d39e4325183c7fbc9def77403046: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen15973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15974" type="x-p"/> For the thing which I greatly reared - Literally, the fear that I feared; or, I feared a fear, as in the margin. While I was in prosperity I thought adversity might come, and I had a dread of it. I feared the loss of my family and my property; and both have occurred. I was not lifted up: I knew that what I possessed I had from Divine Providence, and that he who gave might take away. I am not stripped of my all as a punishment for my self-confidence.
entries.aca10a5f15f44da634799790f7d5ef1a5315dcfd: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen15974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15975" type="x-p"/> I was not in safety - If this verse be read interrogatively, it will give a good and easy sense: Was I not in safety? Had I not rest? Was I not in comfort? Yet trouble came. It is well known that, previously to this attack of Satan, Job was in great prosperity and peace. Mr. Good translates, I had no peace; yea, I had no rest. Yea, I had no respite, as the trouble came on; and refers the whole to the quick succession of the series of heavy evils by which he was tried. There is a similar thought in the Psalmist: Deep crieth unto deep at the noise of thy water-spouts; all thy waves and thy billows have gone over me; <reference osisRef="Psa.42.7">Psa 42:7</reference>. One evil treads on the heels of another. <div eID="gen15975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15976" type="x-p"/> In this chapter Job's conflict begins. Now, and not before, Satan appears to have access to his mind. When he deprived him of his property, and, what was still dearer, of his sons and his daughters, the hope of his family, he bore all with the most exemplary patience, and the deepest resignation to the Divine will. When his adversary was permitted to touch his body, and afflict it in the most grievous and distressing manner, rendered still more intolerable by his being previously deprived of all the comforts and necessaries of life; still he held fast his integrity; no complaint, no murmur was heard. From the Lord's hand he received his temporal good; and from that hand he received his temporal evil, the privation of that good. Satan was, therefore, baffled in all his attempts; Job continued to be a perfect and upright man, fearing God, and avoiding evil. This was Job's triumph, or rather the triumph of Divine grace; and Satan's defeat and confusion. <div eID="gen15976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15977" type="x-p"/> It is indeed very seldom that God permits Satan to waste the substance or afflict the body of any man; but at all times this malevolent spirit may have access to the mind of any man, and inject doubts, fears, diffidence, perplexities, and even unbelief. And here is the spiritual conflict. Now, their wrestling is not with flesh and blood - with men like themselves, nor about secular affairs; but they have to contend with angels, principalities and powers, and the rulers of the darkness of this world, and spiritual wickednesses in heavenly places. In such cases Satan is often permitted to diffuse darkness into the understanding, and envelope the heavens with clouds. Hence are engendered false views of God and his providence, of men, of the spiritual world, and particularly of the person's own state and circumstances. Every thing is distorted, and all seen through a false medium.
